title: A landing, in six moves
caption: Please do not press the abort button.
footnote: The descent stage is still on display at the site. No visiting hours.

steps.label: Eagle undocks
steps.detail: The lander leaves Columbia, the ship that stays in orbit.

arrow.label: Look it over
arrow.detail: Collins checks Eagle from Columbia's window.

steps.label: Lower the orbit
steps.detail:
A 30-second burn behind the Moon.
The low point drops to about 15 km.

arrow.label: Coast down
arrow.detail: About an hour of falling, engine off.

steps.label: Powered descent
steps.detail:
The engine fires again to brake.
Twelve minutes to the surface.

arrow.label: Computer falls behind
arrow.detail: A radar that isn't needed keeps sending it work.

parts.label: Brake
parts.detail: The engine fires against the direction of travel to shed orbital speed.

parts.label: Approach
parts.detail: Eagle pitches upright, so the crew can see where they are heading.

parts.label: Final descent
parts.detail: The pilot picks the spot; the computer holds the rate of descent.

risks.label: Landing long
risks.detail:
Landmarks pass early.
Eagle will come down beyond the planned spot.

steps.label: 1202 and 1201 alarms
steps.detail:
The computer is overloaded.
It drops minor jobs and keeps steering.
Mission Control says go.

branch.label: Abort to orbit
branch.detail:
Not taken.
Eagle would have climbed back to Columbia.

arrow.label: If steering stops
arrow.detail: A computer that stopped guiding meant an abort.

arrow.label: Keep going
arrow.detail: Eagle tips upright. The crew can see the ground.

steps.label: Armstrong takes over
steps.detail:
The autopilot is heading for a crater full of boulders.
He flies past it.

arrow.label: Find flat ground
arrow.detail: Low-fuel calls count down while he looks.

risks.label: Dust hides the ground
risks.detail: The engine blows dust across the surface in the last metres.

steps.label: Eagle touches down
steps.detail:
Sea of Tranquility, 20:17 UTC.
Under a minute of fuel left.

summary: How Eagle got from orbit to the surface, and the alarm that nearly stopped it.
